o: It encrypts user passwords before they travel on the network
It lets third-party apps access resources without sharing passwords
It replaces TLS as the way to protect HTTP traffic in transit
It defines how user passwords should be stored in a database
questions.x: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. Third-party apps receive authorization codes and access tokens instead of the user password, so access can be limited and later revoked.
questions.h: The valet-key analogy is about limited access. What does the app receive instead of the real password?

questions.q: Who are the three main parties in an OAuth 2.0 flow?
o: The client, a reverse proxy, and the resource owner
The end user, an attacker, and the application database
Resource owner, client application, and OAuth provider
The web browser, a REST API, and the session store
questions.x: The resource owner is the user. The client application is the site that wants access, such as a blog. The OAuth provider, also called the authorization server, authenticates the user and issues tokens.
questions.h: Think who owns the data, who wants access to it, and who issues the token after login.

questions.q: Which statement about OAuth 2.0 is correct?
o: None of these statements are true
OAuth shares the real user password
The client receives the user password
Access tokens expire after a short time
questions.x: Access tokens expire after a short time, like a valet key. OAuth does not share the password, and the client never receives it. None is wrong because that expiry claim is true.
questions.h: Compare the valet-key idea. Do access tokens last forever, or only for a limited time?

questions.q: In the authorization code flow, what does the provider send in the redirect?
o: A short-lived authorization code later exchanged for an access token
The user password, already hashed, so the client can log in as them
The access token itself, placed in the URL for the browser to keep
A client_secret the browser should keep as a permanent session cookie
questions.x: After consent, the provider redirects to redirect_uri with a code. The client then exchanges that code server-to-server for an access token. The code is short-lived and single-use. The access token is not shown in the browser.
questions.h: The flow is two steps. What travels in the browser redirect, and what is fetched only on the back channel?

questions.q: Why is the authorization code exchanged on the back channel?
o: So the user can type the code into a second login form
So the access token is never exposed in the user browser
So the provider can skip consent and issue tokens silently
So the client_id can be omitted from the first redirect
questions.x: The code is visible in the redirect but expires quickly and can be used only once. The access token, which actually grants access, is exchanged server-to-server and never appears in the browser.
questions.h: If the access token appeared in the redirect URL, who else might see it?
